references.text: Elijah called down fire from heaven on messengers sent by King Ahaziah. James and John seem to have this event in mind when they ask Jesus if they should call down fire from heaven on the Samaritans.
Elijah called down fire from heaven for the third time. The disciples wanted to do the same as Elijah did, but Jesus rejected this attitude.
Fire went out from the Lord and consumed the 250 men who were offering incense. An example of God's judgment by fire from heaven in the OT.
The Lord rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah from heaven and destroyed the cities. Another foreshadowing of divine fire falling from heaven to destroy.

Jesus had just rebuked the disciples for stopping someone who was casting out demons in his name—a context where the disciples show an exclusive and judgmental attitude, which is continued here in their desire to punish the Samaritans.
Jesus rebuked James and John and rejected their wish to call down fire. This shows that Jesus' mission was not to destroy human lives but to save them.
Jesus called James and John "Boanerges," which means "sons of thunder." Their temperament is clearly shown in their desire to call down fire from heaven.
Instead of wishing judgment on those who rejected him, Jesus wept over Jerusalem. A contrast to the disciples' wish to destroy the village.
Samaritans and Jews did not associate with each other, which provides background for the rejection by the Samaritan village and the disciples' strong reaction.
The Lord sent fire and consumed Elijah's offering. In the OT, fire from heaven is a well-known sign of God's judgment, and this is what the disciples want to repeat.
